Temporal Core Migration¶

Decision¶

The public Pluss value system converges on four core types:

Type

Meaning

Series

Numeric, boolean, and differentiable values

Note

Textual, byte, token, and language-oriented values

Timeline

Absolute instants interpreted through a timezone and calendar

Duration

Signed elapsed quantities represented at nanosecond precision

TimeIndex is not a fifth value kind. It is the role played by a rank-one Timeline when an operation needs an ordered temporal axis. Its public contract therefore moves to Timeline::index().

Duration remains the fourth type rather than being renamed to Period. A period is an anchored calendar concept whose length can depend on its position and timezone; a duration is an elapsed quantity. If Pluss later needs anchored periods, that concept requires a separate contract instead of changing the meaning of Duration.

Public Index Contract¶

Timeline::index() is the canonical validation boundary:

const auto checked = timeline.index();       // rank one and non-decreasing
const auto unchecked = timeline.index(false); // rank one; ordering unchecked

The returned accessor owns a cheap Timeline handle. Construction validates the requested contract once, and all operations invoked through that accessor reuse the validated state:

const auto index = timestamps.index();

const auto position = index.searchsorted(key);
const auto previous = index.asof(key);
const auto bins = index.resample_bins(options);
const auto joined = index.join_asof(other.index());

Rank validation is constant-time. Monotonic validation is linear in the number of timestamps, but is paid once for a retained accessor rather than by every index operation.

A permanent monotonicity cache must not be attached to Timeline storage yet. Timeline::from_buffer() can borrow mutable external memory, and writes made through the external owner cannot update a Timeline mutation generation. Caching inside the accessor is safe because it describes the storage state that the caller explicitly validated. Callers must not mutate borrowed storage while using an accessor whose ordering contract depends on that storage.

Internal Engine¶

The existing TimeIndex implementation is retained as the initial index engine. This avoids rewriting proven search, as-of join, alignment, rolling, and resampling kernels while the public ownership model changes.

The intended end state is:

Public
  Timeline
  Timeline::index() -> TimelineIndexAccessor

Internal
  pluss::codeh::detail::TimeIndexEngine

Migration proceeds in compatibility-preserving stages:

  1. Add Timeline::index() and route it through the existing validation and TimeIndex kernels.

  2. Make new code use timeline.index().method().

  3. Retain public TimeIndex, pluss::timeindex::*, and pluss::make_timeindex(...) temporarily as compatibility forwarders.

  4. Change exported PlussMic APIs to accept Timeline; operations requiring an index call .index() at their boundary.

  5. Merge PlussMic’s Timeline and TimeIndex payload alternatives.

  6. Decode legacy serialized TimeIndex values as Timeline while writing only the Timeline representation for new data.

  7. Remove the public TimeIndex type, factories, exports, and documentation.

  8. Move the retained implementation behind TimelineIndexAccessor as detail::TimeIndexEngine.

Compatibility names are transitional, not permanent aliases. The migration is complete only when public headers and generated documentation no longer expose TimeIndex as a value type.

PlussMic Duration Contract¶

PlussMic currently stores Series, Note, Timeline, and TimeIndex as separate payload alternatives. The final payload set becomes:

Series
Note
Timeline
Duration

Removing TimeIndex therefore creates the runtime-type position needed by Duration without increasing the number of payload alternatives. Index status belongs to DataFrame/Thread axis metadata and operation contracts, not to a column’s value dtype.

Duration integration must define behavior throughout PlussMic rather than merely adding it to a variant:

Area

Required contract

Loading and serialization

Preserve signed nanoseconds and lane-wise NaT

Display

Render elapsed quantities, never timestamp calendar text

Arithmetic

Preserve Duration for duration addition and subtraction

Temporal algebra

Timeline - Timeline -> Duration; Timeline +/- Duration -> Timeline

Ratios

Duration / Duration -> Series

Comparison

Compare duration values with shape and absence rules preserved

Reduction

Sum, mean, minimum, and maximum return Duration where meaningful

Structure

Filtering, grouping, reshaping, and concatenation preserve dtype

Casting

Keep elapsed quantities distinct from epoch timestamps

Legacy TimeIndex serialization tags remain readable during the transition but are promoted to Timeline immediately after decoding. Enum values and persisted tags must not be silently reused for Duration.

Completion Criteria¶

The migration is complete when:

  • public Pluss exposes exactly Series, Note, Timeline, and Duration as core value types;

  • every index operation is reached through Timeline::index();

  • PlussMic has no TimeIndex payload, kind, cast target, or public overload;

  • PlussMic supports Duration across storage, I/O, display, arithmetic, comparison, reduction, grouping, and reshaping;

  • old serialized TimeIndex data loads as Timeline;

  • Queue and PlussTils no longer register TimeIndex and continue to register Duration; and

  • compatibility factories and TimeIndex documentation have been removed.

Current Checkpoint¶

The compatibility phase is active. Timeline::index() is public and its TimelineIndexAccessor name currently aliases the proven TimeIndex engine, so new source and documentation use the accessor contract without duplicating kernels or invalidating existing TimeIndex consumers. The complete handwritten TimeIndex method family has moved to the timeline-index documentation family; the old landing page now exists only to explain the transition.

Duration is now a first-class payload through the initial PlussMic structural boundary:

  • Thread, Stream, Slot, Registry, and Catalog preserve Duration kind, signed nanoseconds, lane order, and validity;

  • explicit casts support Duration to Int64 nanoseconds or Note text and Int64 or exact decimal-nanosecond Note values back to Duration, while Duration-to-Timeline is rejected;

  • shared scalar formatting, comparison, append, sorting, extrema, alignment, group hashing, and distinct counting have Duration policies;

  • DataFrame null allocation, cast routing, exact join keys, category decode, reshape concatenation, axis matching, matrix(), pivot materialization, fillnull, and replace preserve Duration;

  • BI scalar and inclusive-range filters carry typed Duration bounds, compare through Duration semantics, and serialize bounds as exact signed nanoseconds;

  • CSV, Excel, SQLite, JSON emission, and Arrow/Parquet adapters have explicit Duration branches; Arrow uses its native nanosecond Duration type, while text-schema ingestion requires exact decimal nanoseconds rather than unit guessing; and

  • display, diagnostics, catalog alignment, Nexus labels, and modal reduction retain Duration identity and treat NaT as absence.

Public TimeIndex remains available at this checkpoint. The remaining work is to finish Duration arithmetic and the remaining reduction policies across PlussMic, verify the Arrow branch in an Arrow-enabled build, migrate exported Timeline/TimeIndex alternatives to Timeline plus index-role metadata, read legacy TimeIndex serialization as Timeline, and only then remove the compatibility type, factories, enum alternatives, and old landing page.
